utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. I don't notice any absences amongst the Defence teams. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. All right. I think there are some preliminaries, according to what we have been told. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning, colleagues in the courtroom. Indeed, Mr. President, with your leave I would like to address the Trial Chamber concerning the Prosecution's motion filed on the 14th of May in the afternoon, as mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, as mentioned yesterday, as a follow-up to the filing of the Prosecution motion requesting protective measures for Witness PW-108, which included for the first time, as you know, disclosure of an interview conducted with the witness, as well as a summary which was prepared along the lines of Rule 65 ter, we have met with our client at the Detention Unit yesterday, with a view to, first, taking stock of this new material and, number 2, assessing its impact on the ability of the accused, Drago Nikolic, to conduct his defence. As a result of this consultation process, I am now in a position to state that more than ever we are of the view that serious prejudice to the accused Drago Nikolic results from this Prosecution motion. Accordingly, we have decided to file a motion for reconsideration of two decisions rendered by the Trial Chamber on 6 December 2006 and 9 February 2007. As will be seen from this motion, which we hope to file no later than tomorrow, 17 May, because it does require some preparation and we are not in a position to do it today, our objective is to have this witness, namely P108 [sic], removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give me a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bourgon, if you are going to file a motion, we prefer not to hear anything further from you and wait for the motion and then hear what the Prosecution has to say and then decide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we believe that I need, and that is my -- the aim of my -- of what I wish to say this morning, is to highlight the context of this motion, which is necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need to hear it now, Mr. Bourgon. So I suggest that you sit down, unless you have anything else to state which is not related to the motion. You sit down and prepare the motion and let us -- let it take its normal course. We don't want to hear submissions on a motion that hasn't still been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will then not speak about the motion but simply tell you or inform the Trial Chamber, which is the aim of what I wish to say this morning, that we believe that this is a serious motion but why I want to address the Trial Chamber orally this morning before the motion is to inform the Trial Chamber that as a result of this motion that we will file, we will be asking the Court not to proceed with 13 witnesses, because we are no longer ready to cross-examine these witnesses. And I can inform you the numbers of these witnesses or I can sit down and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, stop, please. Mr. Bourgon, sit down. We've heard enough on this. Please file your -- prepare and file your motion and it will be dealt with in due course. Finished. Let's get this new witness, please, unless there are other preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this witness that we -- is about to enter the courtroom amongst those 13 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was about to inform that because of this witness, because he's already here and as a gesture of goodwill, we want to proceed and we will proceed with this witness, with the caveat that he may be recalled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- at a later points for further cross-examination. Mr. President, I want to put on the record that I disagree with being prevented from addressing the Court this morning on such an important issue that goes directly to the rights of the accused. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is our conclusion. Please come forward with your motion and we will give it... Mr. Thayer, if it's about this motion or about what Mr. Bourgon stated then leave it and incorporate what you have to say in your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I wouldn't dare at this point, Mr. President. I have one exhibit from yesterday to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm coming to that. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just before the tender process, Your Honour, I want the Trial Chamber to be on alert that the Defence of Ljubisa Beara also joins Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no problems with motion. That is your right and we'll give each motion due consideration. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is one more thing I need to say at this point and it is simply that there is one issue that needs to be determined before the motion is filed, and I've asked my colleague this morning to inform me whether annex C, which was joined to the motion in August, which was filed by the Prosecution, that was an ex parte motion given to the Trial Chamber, whether this annex C is the same as annex B which was given to the Trial Chamber in December. I've asked my colleague and I require this information before we can file the motion, and Mr. President, I wish to add that this motion for the sake of judicial expediency could be done also orally tomorrow morning if that was the wish of the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the points involved are serious enough to merit a written motion. Can you give Mr. Bourgon an answer to his query?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can, Mr. President. Since my friend's inquiry we have looked at the document in question. I believe we can disclose it confidentially. It is substantially the same information that has been disclosed during the course of yesterday's proceeding with the exception of a bottom part of the document which is not pertinent to the witness at all. It concerns a completely different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the August one covered more than one person. All right. So let's bring in the next witness. Mr. Bourgon, if you require more than tomorrow for the filing of the motion, you will have more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We will do as quickly as we can, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we bring in the witness, documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one exhibit with respect to the last witness it's P00377, the operations duty officer notebook. The exhibit had been mistakenly identified in e-court as being previously admitted through PW-104. We have double checked. It has not. So at this time we would offer the exhibit in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It's not fully translated. It's been translated in three tranches. It's a document that runs to 188 pages. And it's been translated - I can give the ERN numbers - 46 pages the first time, seven pages the second time, and three pages the third. Accordingly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's 56 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Less than a third of it has been translated, and I know because we have been in discussion, if we leave it marked for identification purposes, it will remain marked for identification purposes probably until we've all packed up our bags and left this Tribunal because we have all of us trying to persuade the translation service to translate the whole document without any success. Accordingly, I believe it's inappropriate to admit the whole of this document, all 188 pages of it, as an exhibit. What I've suggested to the Prosecution is that they give to each of the translated passages or portions new 65 ter numbers, and that they are then admitted into evidence and there would be no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The complicating factor is we have had certain pages of it translated that are not within the Prosecution's sections that are translated and we've had to go back through the exhibits that you have rejected for tendering on the basis that P377 was in evidence when it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's my suggestion as to how to deal with P377, and without being overly technical, I do object to it being admitted in its entirety because it's not a language of the Tribunal, but I also in due course will have to ask you to admit certain passages which we've put to witnesses in the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with the objection, first. Yes, what's your position on what has been suggested --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can certainly have the entire notebook translated. We will coordinate with our friends to get that done. I understand that there has been some other portions that have already been translated. We will work with them to translate the entire notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, and again it's based on our ignorance of what supposedly could happen in the future. This document has been made use of already by -- during the testimony of other witnesses. Is it-- are you planning, either you or any of the Defence teams, to make use of it any further with other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it's also the case of having it translated within a specified time limit. Not just in a vacuum. You said -- you spoke with some authority, as if you are sure that you can have it translated. How far does that go?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we push, Your Honour, we have managed to get pretty big projects done. I'll have to check to find out what the realistic estimate is, what we are really talking about, but we will do everything we can to get it translated. We've done that before with other large projects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime until this is done and hopefully this is done at the earliest and in time for it being able to be used for future witnesses if possible, do you object to the proposition of Mr. Haynes to have the parts that are already translated admitted with three different 65 ter numbers and then eventually 377 will replace them?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No. At this point, I think that we can work with that, Your Honour. No objection at this point to that. It's not the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll give the floor to Mr. Meek first and then deal with the matter. It's all -- you're still on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours we object, the Defence of Ljubisa Beara, we object to the admission of this on several grounds. First, it has not been translated. Secondly, there has been no showing of chain of custody. Thirdly, the witness who previously testified,(redacted), who mentioned this notebook, only testified he saw his name in it and a phone number. The witness yesterday only -- only testified in regards to two pages in his own handwriting and if you recall his testimony, he didn't know anything about other entries, he didn't know who made those entries, he's not an expert, he said, he couldn't tell us a lot of things, so again, there has been no foundation for this document, no authenticity and no chain of custody. It should not be admitted at this point, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm only standing to seek a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that person did not have protective measures, did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, he absolutely did, Your Honour, and I believe my friend was referring --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, Mr. Meek. Still I remind you that yesterday, for example, you went practically through the entire notebook with the witness, drawing his attention to where it was -- where entries in pencil, entries in pen, asking about handwriting, asking about this and about that. So our answer to all the submissions that have been made, submission to admit and objections from Mr. Haynes and from Mr. Meek is that for the time being, this is not being admitted; it is being marked for identification. Once we have the full translation, there will only be left the question of authenticity and chain of command that has been brought up, et cetera. So the document will remain marked for identification, not only until it is translated but until these two issues also are dealt with and determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to follow up on your previous query, Mr. President, we will be, in addition to bringing witnesses who will discuss various portions of the notebook, as my friends know,

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: (redacted) So there are many questions that I believe will be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon has left the courtroom? Yes, Ms. Nikolic, he went to prepare the motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to leave -- Mr. Bourgon has left and he's working from the office. He's working on the submission so as to be able to file it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He should be thankful we gave him more time. Yes, let's bring the witness now. I'm sorry, you had some --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My apologies to you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not at all. Through the last witness, I would tender into evidence 7D180. It is a page from the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Mr. Haynes, is it not page 36 of P377?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may very well be but it's a portion that is untranslated and we had it translated separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it was translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, you're quite correct, yes. I stand corrected on that, but through the previous witness, there was 7D155 and 7D159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you tendering exactly, 7D180 and through the previous witness, 155 and 159?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 155 and 159, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. As regards 155 and 159, do they form part of 377? And have they been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. So I don't think there is a need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since these are part of 377 in any case, our decision is to have them all marked temporarily for identification. The reason being the points raised by Mr. Meek now, because there is the possibility of this document not being admitted at all. Do you follow, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I do. I'm not going to argue any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the position. These three will remain marked for identification pending a decision on whether 377 will be admitted or whether it should remain -- or whether it should be thrown out of the records. Anyone else wishes to tender documents? Okay. There are no protective measures for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This witness will need a caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to welcome you to this courtroom, where you are about to start giving evidence. Madam Usher is going to give you a piece of paper with the text of a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth, that you are required to make before you start giving evidence according to our rules. Please go ahead, read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable, take a seat. You're here to answer questions that will be put to you first by the Prosecution, per Mr. McCloskey, whom you've already met and then by the various members of the Defence teams. You have lived part of the events that you are going to testify about, and my responsibility here is to alert you, to make you aware of certain rights that you have as a witness. Your obligation normally is that you answer each question that is put to you fully and truthfully but there may be some questions asked sometimes which you feel that, if you are answer them, you may be exposing yourself to possible criminal proceedings later on. I don't know if this will be the case or not but I'm just giving you a piece of advice that I am required to do under the rules. If questions are put to you that, if answered by you, truthfully, would -- could possibly expose you to criminal proceedings or could possibly incriminate you in any manner, then you have a right under our rules to ask us to be exempted from answering such questions. This is a right that you have. But it is not an absolute right. It's a limited right. We have two options. We can either decide, after hearing you and possibly other submissions, to indeed exempt you from answering such questions, or we can compel you to answer such questions. If we do compel you to answer such questions, however, you have an ulterior right, namely that whatever you state in answering those questions, provided you're telling us the truth, that information cannot be used against you in any future proceedings that could be taken in your regard. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And have you -- had you been informed about this right before? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can safely proceed. I expect you to be here today and tomorrow. We won't finish with you today. I don't see the testimony of this witness finishing today. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience; sometimes we take longer than we expect. First, can you tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Ostoja Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 12th -- or the 2nd of December, 1951 in Fojnica. I was raised in Fojnica and up to 1980, upon completion of school, I worked in Fojnica. As of 1980 to 1992 I was in the territory of Kalesija in Memici village where I worked at school until 1992. From 1992, onwards, I was mobilised and up to 1995, I was a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get into a little more detail about that, but can you tell us what -- how you wound up in school, what kind of schooling you took?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I am a PE teacher. I completed higher education in physical education. I have a degree in physical education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me skip to what you do now. What work do you do now, especially in the winter?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I have a car wash, and in the winter I spend about three months every year on mount Jahorina. I teach people to ski. I'm a ski trainer, a ski instructor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you do your regular mandatory JNA service?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the JNA. I went to the school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long were you in the JNA and when?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I served from 1977 to 1978, a total of 12 months. That was my regular compulsory military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what area were you working during that year? Sorry, not physical location but what sort of military work were you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about my compulsory military service, where I served then, or later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just the compulsory right now. Just what branch were you in during your compulsory?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Infantry, the school for reserve officers, infantry. Upon the completion of my training, lasting seven months, I was given a rank of a Sergeant. Then I was reassigned and then we were assigned either to be commanders of squads or commanders of platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at the end of your mandatory year, did you stay in the reserves and continue to be connected in some way to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon completion of my regular military service, I returned to my workplace and I was a member of the reserve forces in Fojnica, and I occupied the position of the security organ there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe, during the peacetime period, what does reserve service involve? How often do you actually become engaged in that work?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It all depended on various things. There were manoeuvres, for example, between 1978 and 1992, I spent a month or a month and a half in training as a member of peacetime units, as a member of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's now jump ahead to 1992. Before the war got going in Bosnia, what were you doing for a living?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I taught at school. I was a PE teacher at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you become mobilised at some point in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, there was general mobilisation and that is when I became a member of the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At what rank did you begin in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I started as a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us just a very brief outline of your career in the VRS from 1992 to just up to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I worked as a security organ for a short period of time, up to the fall of the 6th Battalion when an attack was launched on Glodjansko Brdo. And then I was appointed the battalion commander. From that moment on, I would act as a deputy battalion commander or battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly what date you became a battalion commander for the 6th Battalion? It can be rough. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It was in 1995. I acted as a commander for six or seven months of that year or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in July 1995, were you the commander of the 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where was the 6th Battalion headquarters located in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, the command of the 6th Battalion was in the village of Petkovci, in the old school, next to it is a building, a residential building, for teachers. And actually we used one of those flats in that residential building as the seat of my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I showed you an aerial photo in my office. Were you able to mark where you believe those -- the building was?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you -- I'm going to show you a copy of that just so we can establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be P02815. This is a what-- a bit of a different aerial than we have used before but I provided it to the Defence a few days ago, after he marked it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As we are waiting for that to come up, can you tell us just generally what was your area that -- of responsibility for the 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The defence sector of the 6th Battalion was the right bank of the Sapna river and to the left from Baljkovacka Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in July 1995, can you tell us about how many men you had in the 6th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The battalion had approximately 400 men. However, about 120 men were on the line, or maybe up to 150. In other words, between 120 and 150 men were in the trenches on the defence lines of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. This photo has come up and we notice that there are two places marked. Does this look like the photo that you marked in my office?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you first tell us what number 1 is? You might zoom in a bit more on one and two. Thank you. Do you recognise that building you circled as number 1?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the residential building. Before the war, it was used by teachers, and during the war as well, teachers were living in that building. In the lower part of the building, i.e. in the -- on the ground floor, there was an empty apartment, an apartment that had been vacated, and this is where my command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'd also asked you to circle the new school in Petkovci. Did you do that? Do you see that on this photo?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that marked number 2?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll -- as you know, we'll talk about that a little later. All right. Let's now go to the 14th of July, which is I know a date you've talked about before. But on the 14th of July, had any of your men been attached with Vinko Pandurevic, to have gone down to the Srebrenica operation, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of July, in the morning, I received a call from the chief, from Dragan Obrenovic. I was asked to send 40 men to the brigade command, to the Standard barracks. They were to join the units that had been deployed in Snagovo. The mission was to defend Zvornik and the Serbian villages located in that sector; in the sector of Snagovo there were Serbian villages. I asked him not to take my soldiers if at all possible because an attack had been expected on that axis by the Muslim forces. However, he called me again and told me that I had to send 40 men to the Standard. That was his order. I did that. I gathered my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you briefly. Do you know where Obrenovic was when he spoke to you over the phone?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. We spoke via radio. Later on, however, I learned that he was somewhere in the Snagovo sector when he called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said he's called you twice. Do you remember roughly the time of day on the 14th that you received the first call from him?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Possibly between 8.00 and 9.00. And the second call came maybe an hour or an hour and a half later, after the first call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you -- pardon me if you've said this, but were you at your command post at Petkovci where you received this radio communication?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I was on the defence lines at a forward command post, an IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe what kind of communication you had at your forward command post?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I had induction means of communication, and a radio communication, RUP 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the induction communication, that was a hard line, hard wire?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, hard-line telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did that wire go to from your IKM?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: All the battalions had their battalion switchboards. They were all at the commands of the respective battalions. Not in the commander's office, but all over the battalion, the signalsmen had their own premises, they had a switchboard there, and through that switchboard, communications were established with the defence lines. All platoon commanders, company commanders, and the forward command post were linked via that telephone line. At the same time, the telephone line existed between my command and the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the induction line you're talking about too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the telephone induction line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a civilian PTT line at your forward command post?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you spoke with Obrenovic that morning, you said it was on the radio. So was it on the RUP that you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, RUP 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember if you spoke to him directly, or whether it was perhaps a signalsman or a radio person passing on the conversation or do you remember speaking to him directly?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Chief Obrenovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think I interrupted you when you were saying you were gathering your men to take them to Standard. Can you continue telling us about that? About what time did you start gathering your men to go to Standard?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the second call. It could have been 10.00 or half past 10.00. I called my company commanders and asked them to choose a number of men from each trench. They gathered and sometime between 11.00 and 12.00, they assembled. One part of the unit was gathered in Kitovnica and another part in Petkovci. They were all transported to Standard sometime before 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go with them?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I went there because I was in the defence sector of the 6th Battalion. I took the battalion car and the soldiers were transported in a small TAM lorry. The other group arrived from Petkovci, so I handed those 40 men over at Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see Major Obrenovic at Standard that day?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, no at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you learn that day where he was?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. At Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me ask you a question I've asked before but I think it was a little confusing so you may have misunderstood it. Going back to early July, Vinko Pandurevic took a group down to Srebrenica, didn't he, to take part in that operation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have to give any of your men to assist the Commander Pandurevic in that operation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was supposed to send 40 men, i.e. a platoon, with their commander to Srebrenica. They were first brought to Standard, handed over to the brigade command, and then they were placed under the command of the commander of the unit that was engaged in fighting in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So by 14 July, when you've given another 40 men, are your units stretched pretty thin up at the defence sector?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I've told you that the strength of the battalion was about 400 men, but I could not send half of the unit for vacation, so I had to recall my men who were on furlough in order to reinforce our lines, in order to bring up the units on the defence lines up to strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you recall your men from furlough?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Some men were recalled even before the 14th, i.e. when the unit had been sent to Srebrenica, and since Kitovnica is very close, usually men were from that village, also from Brnjica, which had been known as Djulici. This is where the soldiers resided. So it was easy for me to replenish my unit by recalling the men from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember what day you recalled them? Was it before you took the 40 to Standard or after?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: After. I recalled them once men had left for Standard, and then I reinforced the trenches to meet the minimum criteria of at least three men per one trench for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when -- roughly what time did you leave Standard on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Between 1300 and 1400 hours. I went back to my defence positions, to my forward command post. I had a briefing with my company commanders, and I stayed there sometime up to between 1700 and 1800 hours, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember, was anyone with you when you went from Standard back to your forward command post?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, it's quite possible that the courier was with me, the driver, but I often drove myself. So I can't really recall whether this man was with me at that time or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was your driver that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Vlado Josic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At the time hat you were at Standard did you hear anything about any prisoners, Muslim prisoners located around the schools in the area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you were at your forward command post until about how late that day? I'm sorry. Sorry, after -- from Standard you went to your forward command post, how long were you there at your forward command post on the afternoon of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, up until maybe 1700 hours. It was in the afternoon. Now, I don't know whether it was 1700 hours, 1800 hours. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you receive any information when you -- well, where did you go when you left your forward command post?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I went back to the battalion command in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive any information when you got back there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, down there, I met my deputy, Marko Milosevic, and he told me that he had been told that some prisoners were supposed to arrive at the Petkovci school, and -- however, he had received this call earlier and by the time I arrived there, the prisoners were already in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your deputy tell you who he received this call from?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: From the duty operations officer in the brigade. This man told him that the prisoners were supposed to arrive there, allegedly to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Marko Milosevic, your deputy, have any information about these prisoners that were to be exchanged, how many of them?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't know their number, and he didn't know the number of vehicles that was supposed to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what's the next thing that happened after you got this report?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: After that, there was a call from the brigade. Colonel Beara was supposed to be notified that he should report to the command. I asked, "Where, what command?" And the duty officer said, "Well, he knows well which command he's supposed to report to."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you said that there was a call from the brigade. Who took the call?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I took the call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were you speaking to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The duty operations officer. It was Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when he told you that Colonel Beara was supposed to be notified, did you know who Colonel Beara was?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't know Colonel Beara at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. I'll look at the other one as well, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. On the LiveNote, we are not receiving the transcript any further, while it's still scrolling on the main monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Should I just keep going and see what happens? Are they getting it okay now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends. If we get the okay from the parties, yes. Otherwise, no. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There it goes again. I'm sorry, I apologise. Anyway, last week we just disconnected and reconnected and it worked. We could try that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. My question was still, since the transcript is still rolling on the other monitor, can we proceed while the technicians try to fix the e-court or do you -- because, for example, last time I heard someone saying, yeah, but we need to mark --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We kind of need to mark it, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop for a short while. Mr. McCloskey, I apologise to you, I'm sorry, but we can't help it. The technicians, please. I'll try to disconnect and connect again. It didn't work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you disconnect completely and connect again, it gets you back to where we are. All right? But I want to make sure, thank you, Mr. Meek, for letting us know that you have done that already. The other Defence teams, please? Ms. Fauveau is okay; Mr. Lazarevic, the same; Ms. Condon, all right. Does anyone still have the problem? Is any of the accused following the transcript in English? We can proceed? Okay? All right. We can proceed. I think everyone has more or less fixed the problem. Sorry for that interruption, Witness, and Mr. McCloskey. Let's go -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. McCloskey, can I get his rank? He said he started as a captain but what his rank was when he was 6th Battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. In July, can you tell us all what your rank was in 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Captain first class. So it's just one rank higher than the one I started out with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can ask one more question, whether he addressed Obrenovic as Chief Obrenovic, whether it was his way of addressing him or it's a matter of translation. I'd like to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How did you address Major Obrenovic normally?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, normally I would say, "Chief, sir."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The "sir "was always there, I take it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would always say, "Sir" and then I would also use his functional title, "Chief".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On that same subject, how would you address your commander, Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: "Commander, sir."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let's go back to this phone call that you took, and you were told that Colonel Beara, a person you didn't know, was to be informed to call a command. Were you given any other information, for example, where to find this Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that he should be somewhere around the new school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The new school in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in the village of Petkovci, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember anything else from the conversation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I sent the deputy, Milosevic, to go there to the school and to find the colonel, to tell him about the order that I had received, that he should report to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember roughly what time of day it was at this point? Do you know if it was dark or light or --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, it may have been between 1800 and 1900 hours, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did your deputy report back to you later?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. My deputy arrived at the command and he said that he had informed Colonel Beara about the notification that had been received that he should report back to his command, to his command, not the battalion command. That was my mistake. To his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did the -- your deputy tell you that he saw anybody else with Beara?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that Drago Nikolic was also there, the security organ in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anybody else that you recall him mentioning, any other people or troops or anyone else that was with these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: There were some troops, unknown troops, and military police. He was able to identify such because they had white belts. He also said that there had been trucks and buses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "there," what was he referring to, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: There, at the school building, at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he give you an idea of the number of prisoners that were at the school?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me how many prisoners there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he give you an indication of the number of VRS troops or soldiers that were there along with Nikolic and Beara?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't give me the number, but he said that there had been troops there, there at the intersection where they met, but he didn't even go to the school building, so I don't know if there had been any troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know if there is any troops at the school building. But can you tell us what intersection you believe your deputy was telling you that he -- there -- where this occurred?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik-Sapna main road, and a smaller road leading towards the school. So that's the intersection that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where the driveway from the school leads up the main road that's in front of your command post?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, no. The new school was some distance away from the old school, the place where my command post was. It's about 600 to 700 metres. And this is an inhabited area. There are houses there. So this is a village road and at the same time it's the road that's actually leading towards the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we should get that document -- that photograph up again just to clarify it. It's P02815. You can actually now mark on this. The usher will show you. If you can tell from this photograph where you thought they met, maybe we can blow that up a little bit more, one more. Now, I don't know if -- how good you are at understanding these sorts of photographs but can you make out where you think it was that your deputy met Beara and Drago Nikolic? Why don't you put just a big X where you can see it and it will mark it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just put your initials and today's date, which I think is the 16th.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this -- these -- do we see houses along that little road that leads towards the new school?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here at the right-hand side of the road, there are houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were those inhabited at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you just circle the inhabited houses with the pen and we'll finish up with that.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, all those houses here in this area were inhabited. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've made sort of a dotted oval. Thank you. Okay, we can save that. Thanks. Thank you. All right. So you get this report from your deputy. Roughly how long was he away meeting Beara and Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so what, if anything, did you do to check out that situation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything, because I had not received any orders from my command, so there was no need for me to do anything and I had other, more urgent, things to do. I had to deal with the organising. I had to work on improving the combat readiness in my battalion, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So where did you go and what did you do after receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The deputy and myself stayed there for a while, at the battalion command, and then we went back to the defence sector of our battalion, the right wing, the Sapna river area, and we toured the entire line to check out the situation, to verify what the status of the units was, the staffing levels, and whether they had enough ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before going to your front lines, did you hear any noises coming from the area of the new school?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Isolated shots or short bursts, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you do when you heard these short bursts coming from the area of the school and the isolated shots?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what you did that evening of the 15th? You've inspected your lines. Did you meet with any commanding officers or do anything else that evening?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, exactly. I'm not -- I'm jumping ahead of myself. We're still on the 14th. And so you've said you've inspected your lines that early evening. What else did you do? Did you see any commanding officers or anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, as regards the commanding officers from the brigade command, I didn't encounter any of them. I only met with my commanders and we came back quite late to our command in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly what time did you come back that night to your command in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, it may have been at around 2300 hours, 2400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when you got back, did you check on the situation at the school, the new school, I should say?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't go down to the new school at all. It was probably all quiet already. But because I had not received any orders, and there were officers present there from the superior command, there was no need for me to go to the school at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear any noises from the area of the school or elsewhere that drew your attention that night?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, there was gunfire in the depths, from the free territory. It is quite difficult to establish at night where the sound comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were these the sounds of -- that you're used to hearing from the front lines? Can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were these the sounds that you were used to hearing from the front line or were these some sort of different sounds, from what you normally heard at night in that area?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: At that time, there would be sporadic gunfire and short bursts of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe until 1.00 a.m. That's the morning of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: In the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know that hundreds and hundreds of prisoners were being transported from the new school to the Petkovci dam that night?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No idea?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What's the next thing you remember happening? I guess we are now on the 15th, the morning of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning, the 4th Company, in the left wing of my battalion, sustained an attack, a strong attack launched by the Muslim forces, launched from the direction of Nezuk. And a trench was hit at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just for a second. Do you know if that attack was from your front, the 2nd Corps troops, or from your rear, from these guys that were coming through the Snagovo area towards you from the rear?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The attack did not begin on the 15th. The attack started on the 11th and the 12th and they continued. Those were the attacks launched by this 2nd Brigade of the Muslim forces. So it was from the Muslim side, from the front. It was not an attack from our rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So what do you do in that morning of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I sent my deputy, telling him that he should take a few soldiers from the 1st Company on the left wing and check out the situation on the right wing, and if necessary, if any reinforcements were needed, that he should leave those soldiers there until we can assemble some reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where were you when you were issuing these orders?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I was at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly what time of day is it now?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about anything at the new school that day, the 15th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: When I went to the defence sector, to the forward command post, I had gathered up some people, some personnel, from the command, there were some miners there and some soldiers and I took them up there to fill in the gaps on the left flank. And while I was there on the line, I received a call from the battalion communications, telling me that the villagers had come asking for a truck because they had wanted to clean up the school and to drive some bodies, dead bodies, away. I gave my approval for the use of the truck and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is indeed. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We'll have a 25-minute break. I just wish to inform you from the second session onwards, Judge Kwon will preside instead of me, and you will be proceeding pursuant -- we will be proceeding pursuant to 15 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated, Judge Agius will be away on an official business until the end of this week, we will be sitting pursuant to 15 bis. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We left off and you'd been informed that you say some villagers wanted one of your trucks to take away some bodies. What did you learn about these bodies at the new school?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: At that moment, while I was up there on the defence line, there was nothing else, just the call and a request for a lorry for the bodies. That's all I knew at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know whose bodies they were?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I assumed, since Muslim prisoners had been brought there the previous day, that it would be their bodies, that it would be them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No one told you that, you just assumed it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you learn anything else about those bodies or what happened at the school that day on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: On the 15th, I spent the whole day on the defence lines. I had problems with the organisation of the situation in my unit. I did not receive information as to what was going on down there as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Major Obrenovic any time on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him on the 15th. However, I saw him in the morning on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That was on the left wing of the 6th Battalion's defence. As it was pulling out from the positions of the neighbouring battalion, of the 4th Battalion, the Muslim units had already carried out an attack in that area and they had already taken the command of the 4th Battalion on Motovska Kosa. They also took some artillery tools, among them was a Praga and self-propelled mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know that was a very tense and difficult day, but do you recall talking or saying anything to Major Obrenovic about the bodies?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, he stayed there very shortly and in passing by, he informed me that one trench was empty and that they had withdrawn into another trench. I was angry because of that lorry. I told him, "I have a lot of things to do here, and now they are asking me to provide them with a lorry."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say being provided with a lorry, what does -- just what does that have to do with, so it's clear?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, that referred to that call in which I was asked that I should provide a lorry to the civilians for their use, because that area was settled and, as you can see in this image, the houses are very close to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic has said that -- he has reported that you were angry because you had to provide that lorry yourself?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. A lorry had to be allocated from my command and sent away, because the rear of the battalion was in Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've been shown some logs for some -- from some lorries and I mentioned to you that we would go over those briefly, so let's take a look at a couple of logs for lorries, for vehicles from your battalion. If we could go to number -- it should be 303, this is a vehicle log for a truck called a TAM 80, and at the top of it, it has, under the driver, we have a Dragomir Topalovic and Vlado Josic. First of all, can you tell us what a TAM 80 is?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: TAM 80 is a small truck, up to 2 and a half tonnes capacity with a very small driver's cabin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this the kind that has a canvas top over the back?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can it hydraulically dump sand or is it just a straight bed, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. There was no hydraulic device. The bed was made of wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does Dragomir Topalovic, pardon the pronunciation, was he in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his job?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: He was a driver in the logistics platoon. He was in charge of that small lorry and he drove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And also we have Vlado Josic. Is that the same Vlado Josic you've mentioned previously as a courier?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the absence of Topalovic or when he had to go to Srebrenica, then the travel order contained his name, the travel order featured his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you make out who has signed this travel order in the boxes on the right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to devise the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That's all right, if you can't make that out. Let's go now to the segment of the next -- it would be the next page hopefully on the B/C/S and let's go to 15 July. If we could blow that up? We see in the middle of this page, there is what appears to be two segments for the 15 July, and the first one -- can you make out what that first one says? It looks like it's 8.00 to 10.00 and then there is just some --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- slash marks and then what -- under the route, which is that big middle section that lists a lot of villages, can you tell us what it says for the 15th that -- those words, that first one?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Petkovci-Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the next entry is also on the 15th July. The next line down, and it says, 9.00 to 11.00, I believe, and can you read what --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it says?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Brana, what is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That is a separation between the man-made lake and the land. The bauxite factory used that lake for its waste waters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the term, Brana, is -- I don't know how this is going to be translated but Brana is the dam that holds back the -- that lake, that red lake, from the waste waters of the factory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says number of journeys is one of those -- the -- one of the lines where there is a 6, has -- that's number of journeys, if we look at the same 15 July, we go over past the -- what looks like 11 or slash marks and then we see a 6. Is that 6 number of journeys?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what this is a reference to, a TAM 80 taking six journeys to the -- Petkovci and to the dam and then back to Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is that -- what do you believe that is being used for on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain this, because during my second interview with the investigators, I spoke at length about this particular travel order. If the TAM left on the 15th at 8.00 in the direction of Srebrenica, it was absolutely impossible for it to come back to Petkovci at 10.00, and to make six extra journeys between Petkovci, Brana and Crveni Mulj. I know that the TAM left on the 15th in the morning and returned on the 16th to the battalion command, and I really find this totally illogical. I really can't explain how, on the same day, these two impossible things were entered. It was absolutely not possible that these actions had taken place at the same time. The distance between Petkovci and Srebrenica is around 60 kilometres each way, which makes it 120 kilometres for the return journey. These TAM vehicles were not in a very good state of repair and the highest speed that they could achieve was maybe 60 or 70 kilometres. Really, I can't account for these particular entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you explained that to Mr. Manning in your interview of March 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Since he showed you this log, have you cleared this up by speaking to Vlado Josic or Dragomir Topalovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Vlado Josic. I asked him whether he would be able to confirm that he did leave on the 15th to Srebrenica and that he returned on the 16th. He told me that that is correct, that it is exactly that long that that particular TAM vehicle had spent out of the area of responsibilities of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he'd been summonsed to talk to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another vehicle log. It's number 945, I think another one you'd been asked about in that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before then, Mr. McCloskey, can I clarify one thing? Can I draw your attention to page -- let me see -- page 35, line 7 to 8? You put to the witness that whether Mr. Obrenovic said that or he reported the witness was angry. Is it correct that you put that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, I may have misunderstood. My question I believe was supposed to mean not that Mr. Obrenovic was angry but that the witness was angry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it was Mr. Obrenovic who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Obrenovic has said that and he spoke of that subject in response to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we got another -- so we have another vehicle log. In one is for a TAM 75, and we again see the names Dragomir Topalovic and Vlado Josic, and if we go to the next page and we again look at 15 July-- actually, it is -- one second. Sorry, we've got a bit of a mix-up so I'll go on to another question. Sometime before Mr. Obrenovic was arrested, did he speak to you about his -- about these events that you've just testified to, about the time that the Office of the Prosecutor was interviewing people?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Should I answer? When I received my first summons from the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, we had a short conversation -- conversations. Since he had already been interviewed, at one point I asked him whether I would be allowed to say that there was the cleansing operation at the school, which was a notorious fact by then. However, he said that I shouldn't say that. He said that that was something that should not be known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did he mean by that, as far as you know? What was he telling you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this to any accused in this trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the relevance is pretty clear from the questions that -- and I don't know if I need -- if I should get into the facts in front of the witness but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, I think the question is relevant and also it may touch upon the credibility as well. Please go on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us a little -- what did you think Obrenovic was doing? This is about -- before you were going to go speak to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: At that time, he was the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you still in the army?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the army, up to 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what do you think he was doing, calling you in and talking to you about this, telling you not to say anything about the bodies?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I really can't guess what he may have been thinking when he said that. He only let me know that I wasn't supposed to say anything about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did he intimidate you or threaten you or pressure you in any way, aside from what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that before your first interview with the Tribunal, or it the OTP?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was before my first interview with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've said that these -- the cleansing operation at the school became notorious. Were you ever -- did you ever become aware of any investigation into the events related to those bodies or the prisoners at the school by your command or anyone else in 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. We never discussed that, either in the brigade command or elsewhere. I never spoke about these things to any investigators, save for the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you -- did you ever become aware that any member of the Zvornik Brigade was ever punished for any activity related to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: In our brigade, as far as I know, nobody was punished. The first one that was punished was General Krstic, if that is also what you're referring to in your question. In the brigade itself, there was nothing. There were no proceedings taken in that respect. Nobody was punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if I could ask you just for one last explanation, and I think a similar question was probably asked of you in your interview but one may find it rather difficult to believe that you didn't know anything about those prisoners at the school and that the villagers were the ones that you gave the truck to. Can you explain that? How is it that you don't know anything about this and that it's the villagers that got the bodies?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: My battalion command was in Petkovci, and I have told you that the defence sector of the battalion was to the right from the Sapna river and 300 metres from the left from Baljkovacka Potok. In depth, it encompassed Kitovnica and Grbavci villages. Petkovci, as a village did not fall under my defence sector and under my area of responsibility. At the moment when I received the call and when all this was happening, I was at the defence line. In 1992, I was also a member of another battalion, and I experienced a massacre, we had a lot of casualty. That was on Glodjansko Brdo. And I was afraid that the same thing may -- might repeat in Petkovci. That is why I focused on the defence of that area and of the villages in depth, the villages that were inhabited, including Kitovnica, for example. The first houses there were only one kilometre away from the defence line. If the enemy had managed to penetrate through there, then the situation would have been much worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Had there been 500 to a thousand Muslim men in the new school, they would have posed a potential security threat to the village of Petkovci as well, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He's cross-examining his own witness here. This has gone far enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If there were 500 to a thousand prisoners at the Petkovci school, would that have posed a security threat, potentially, to your command in the village of Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's not rephrased at all and it's based on a supposition that's not founded in evidence. It's a question in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely disagree on all counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has difficulty understanding why this amounts to a cross-examination, if not leading, but please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had there been 500 to a thousand Muslim men in that school, would they have posed a potential security threat to your command and the village of Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, when my deputy was informed that the prisoners were coming, he was told that there would be security in place and that our battalion would not be involved, that there was no need for us to be involved in those activities. I therefore saw no need to provide any additional security of the school and the people in the village, the civilians. And this was not my duty, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If prisoners had escaped from that school and killed the village -- people in the house next door to the school, whose responsibility would it have been to protect that house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Fauveau? I think Madam Fauveau was the first to rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question is based on speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And already answered. Let's proceed, Mr. McCloskey, move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you responsible for prisoners that you are aware are located within a kilometre of your battalion, in any way, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness has already answered this question, at page 43, lines 20 to 24, and he also spoke about the responsibilities of his battalion for the school in Petkovci, and the village of Petkovci itself. I think that this has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have -- it calls for a legal conclusion which is inappropriate to ask a witness but I also think that because he's asking this type of question it's clear he's putting the credibility and veracity of this witness at issue which I agree with him on that point, quite candidly. However, I think that maybe it would be prudent at this time to give the instruction again, the caution to the witness if the Court is going to allow this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the need to caution him once again, and just speaking for myself, this question is different from the question previously put. I think. But I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could respond, the responsibility of a soldier is something that this -- does not call for a legal conclusion. They know their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I indicated, this question is different from the previous one and this may relate to his statement -- state of mind at the time so that can be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
