utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic, this will be my last question so we are almost over from this side of things. Are you responsible in any way for prisoners that are housed within a kilometre from you in your village?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, and in accordance with the orders I had received for my battalion to defend an area, the building that you talk about was in the free territory. It was not used for any military purpose on the part of my command, and only civilian structures can be responsible in such a situation for this building. In my view, it was free territory, and I can only defend an area from the rear in case of an attack, such as there was on the 15th and the 16th of July, on the left wing of my battalion. The school was a civilian structure. I couldn't issue an order that it be mobilised, in other words, used for military purposes. That could have been done only by the military department or the brigade command or some instance of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I just remembered one thing I forgot to ask you. On the 15th, did you get a phone call about prisoners again?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: My deputy received a call on the 15th, and he said that the prisoners were supposed to come, Muslim prisoners, and that they had their own security in place and there was no need for us, we did not receive any orders to do anything with regard to the school building. This was just a notification that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I understand that and that's what you said happened on the 14th of July. I'm going now to the next day. Did you receive another call?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The 15th, okay. Yes. On the 15th, I was on the defence lines, and while I was at the forward command post, I received a call telling me that the prisoners should be put in the school building. The man who called me told me he was a security officer. He didn't give me his name. I said that this was not possible, that the prisoners could not be brought to Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The trucks arrived down there. I heard from the locals that the trucks remained there for a while. And then they just turned around and left in an unknown direction. We didn't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you not going to ask whether he told Pandurevic after he arrived about what happened? Shall I ask it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a very good question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to your commander, Vinko Pandurevic, about the events at the school, the bodies and these other things you've been speaking of?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, officially there was no briefing. They did not ask for any information from us about the school and what happened there. I don't recall any official demands, requests, by Mr. Pandurevic, and I don't recall that I actually reported about those events to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't need any official report, and as we've learned from you, you were pretty angry when you spoke to Obrenovic about it. Did you ever in any way officially or unofficially mention these events to Pandurevic? And you may want to think about what you'd said in your interview to Mr. Manning on that subject.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know really. I can't remember whether I told him about that. Probably there was some discussion, but I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just -- I'll read back to you a little bit to see if this helps refresh your recollection at all but it's -- this is page 60 of the English and should be page 65 of the B/C/S. You say that: "After everything was over, sometime after that, there were some spontaneous discussions that occurred where it came up, that I had refused these people to be there and refused to accept them, and I don't know how much they will accept to say that I had indeed informed them about this." Then Mr. Manning says, "So it's your recollection that you did speak about this with Pandurevic?" And you say, "Yes, but I do not recall the exact time."

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that now in my evidence, I told you that I may have spoken to him, but I really don't recall any long or official discussion on this subject. There was no official discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What short, unofficial discussion did you have with Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, I may have told him that there had been some bodies up there, that the school had been cleaned up. This was a notorious fact that the school had been cleaned up and that the tank truck had arrived there to clean up, to wash the area, the platform, in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did he say when you told him this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Witness, Mr. Stanisic. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness stated quite clearly that he may have spoken with Mr. Pandurevic. So I don't see how he can know what Mr. Pandurevic had told him if he is not sure at all that they had in fact spoken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can rephrase the question, whether he may have heard anything from Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you recall, if anything, what Mr. Pandurevic may have responded to your information?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, Mr. Pandurevic was indignant about this whole situation, and all the events in Zvornik, all those things that happened there. So probably in this conversation with me, he must have expressed the same sentiments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did either of you express the sentiments to let's figure out who did this so we are not put to blame?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. There were no such agreements, no orders to that effect, no investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you said -- you answered to Mr. McCloskey that "Mr. Pandurevic was indignant about this whole situation and all the events in Zvornik, all those things that happened there." What would you mean by this, this "all the events in Zvornik"? What did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the killing of those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Who will go first? Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic represents Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, good morning. I'm going to ask you a couple of questions and hopefully it won't take too long but I think it may take an hour or an hour and a half as we predicted just so you have that in mind. My first question to you with respect to the general background: Am I correct that within the 6th Battalion of which you were the commander, there were four companies immediately beneath you, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you describe for me how many men were in each company that was below your 6th Battalion, of which you were a commander?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the list, each company was between 90 and 120 strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I correct -- if I understand your testimony correctly, a fifth battalion was formed from various -- a fifth company was formed from various members of the four companies of your 6th Battalion that were sent to Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. From each company you take out a certain number of men and then you establish a unit as required. If you need a unit that is 40 soldiers strong, then you take ten soldiers from each company and then I send them -- send this unit as requested by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like now to turn your attention to, sir, is the number of interviews that you have had in connection with the Srebrenica enclave. Can you tell us how many interviews you've had with the OTP or any other investigative institution?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I had two interviews regarding the events in Srebrenica with the Office of the Prosecutor from The Hague, and I received a summons from the civilian police in Zvornik to make a statement regarding the events in Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you at any time have any interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor in connection with events other than Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was another interview, again with the investigators from The Hague. It was regarding the Snagovo sector in 1992. But in that period, I was not in the Zvornik Brigade at all, so they did not have proper information, and I myself was unable to give them any information or to tell them anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what I have also but I'll just give you the chronology so that I can be certain about it. Your first interview was on July 28, 2000 and you were identified or summoned to appear for an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor as a witness involving the events of 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And your second interview with the Office of the Prosecutor was July 27th, 2001, approximately a year later, and that involved issues or concerns involving 1992, correct, and not Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, it was about Srebrenica again. In 2002, it was about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Right. March 14th, 2002, it was about Srebrenica. But my question was in between the first and second interview you had an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor on July 27, 2001, and that involved only the period of 1992, which you just testified to in connection with Snagovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us why -- how it is that -- strike that. On March 14, 2002, when you were summoned for a second interview with the office of the Prosecution, did your status change from that which it was on July 28th, 2000, from being a witness to being a suspect?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The interview was halfway done when I -- when my status changed from that of a witness to that of a suspect and then we continued the interview because I agreed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're referring, of course, sir to the first interview, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just jump a little before we get into these meetings that you may have had with certain individuals. You don't know Ljubisa Beara, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, you never met him, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, you never spoke to him, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to your deputy, Marko Milosevic, is it true that the only time you claim that he may have encountered Mr. Beara was on the 14th of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me switch to the meeting that the Prosecution asked you about with Mr. Obrenovic. In his question, he asked, and I'm sure it was somewhat innocently, that before Obrenovic was arrested, you had a meeting with Mr. Obrenovic. Do you remember that he asked you that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to know the meeting that you had with Mr. Obrenovic, was it immediately before he was arrested or was it a longer period of time before his arrest that you had had this meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, I met with Obrenovic before his arrest, while he was still the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you had had this conversation with Mr. Obrenovic about a year before his arrest; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, before I went for the first interview with the investigators from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if I have here that the indictment for Mr. Obrenovic was the 9th of April 2001, and SFOR arrested him on the 15th of April 2001 and we know that your meeting with Mr. Obrenovic happened before your first interview which was July 28th, 2000, it would mean that in fact you met him the year prior, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where did you meet Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic was the brigade commander, and I was a commanding officer in this brigade. I was the battalion commander. And he summoned me to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you stated on page 40, line 3, today, that you had a "short conversation with Mr. Obrenovic". Page 40, line 3. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how short was it? A few minutes? A minute or two?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: 30 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, do you remember when you spoke to Mr. Dean Manning in the Office of the Prosecutor during your second interview involving Srebrenica on March 14th, 2002, you said that the meeting with Mr. Obrenovic, on page 51, counsel, was a one-hour meeting? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, whether it was half an hour long or an hour long, I don't know. But I do remember now that you've mentioned it, that it lasted an hour. However, whether it was half an hour or an hour, I did not have a stop-watch to time it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I could appreciate that, sir. This short one hour or so or half hour to an hour conversation that you had with Mr. Obrenovic, who else was present?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It was just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were working under him in 2000 when this -- when this meeting happened. Do you know if Mr. Obrenovic met with other soldiers to also discuss witnesses' testimony prior to them meeting with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. -- your courier, let me get his name here, Mr. Jovic, did you ask him if Obrenovic spoke to him at any time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you mean Josic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Josic, I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't know that Obrenovic ever spoke to Josic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you ever ask Mr. Josic if Mr. Obrenovic spoke to him, given that you spoke to Mr. Josic about the various logs and lorries that you were questioned today and previously by the office of the Prosecution? Did you ever ask Mr. Josic that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: When I saw these orders on my return from Banja Luka, I did meet up with Josic. He worked in Belgrade at the time, and I had managed to set up a meeting to talk to him and to ask him and to inform him that his name was on the travel order. And I wanted to ask him whether he remembered that he had left for Srebrenica on the 15th and that he had returned on the 16th. This is what I wanted to ask him. And after that, we did not see each other. He works in Belgrade as a civilian. I continued working in the army. So I really don't remember when it was it when I saw him last. I have not seen him in two or three years maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. All I want to know is if you discussed with Mr. Josic whether or not Mr. Obrenovic also met with him in order for him to get his story straight?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet or discuss your interview with your former deputy, Marko Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As for Marko Milosevic, we both reside in Zvornik. We see each other, but we are not very close friends. Still we do maintain contact. However, we have not discussed the events and the second round of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever discuss with Marko Milosevic whether Mr. Obrenovic tried to influence his testimony prior to his interview with the office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Milosevic gave his interview to the office of the Prosecution in connection with the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: We were interviewed on the same day, in Banja Luka, at the same time but in different offices, in two separate offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the second interview of March 14th, 2002, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that in fact you did meet with Mr. Milosevic prior to that second interview so that the both of you can get your story straight as to what you purport occurred on or about the 14th of July 1995. I would be correct, wouldn't I?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: We had to jog each other's memory. It had been a long time ago. However, we never talked in order to coordinate our stories. In my view, it's even impossible for the two of us to have our stories tally 100 per cent. It's impossible for us to agree to tell an identical story.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us when you met with Mr. Milosevic so that you both can have your memory jogged.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Before our departure to Banja Luka, to meet with the investigators. I really can't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So sometime before March 14th, 2002, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Milosevic drive together to Banja Luka for this interview on the 14th of March 2002?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how long of a ride is it that you were together prior to your interview with the office of the Prosecution and Mr. Milosevic's interview?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It takes two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I read, I think carefully, your statement and I'd like you to clarify somethings with me. On page 62 of your second interview you state, and because there is no line number, Your Honour, it's hard to offer that to the Prosecution, but it's there. Page 62, you state, "Many things you learned afterwards, how things went on and what really went on in Petkovci." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll show that to you possibly at the next break because I have only the English version, but is it your testimony, sir, that you did not say that or you just don't recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, just going back briefly to your meeting when conversation with Mr. Obrenovic half hour, hour, whatever that sort conversation was, can you tell us, please, as best as you can recall, what was said during that 30- to 60-minute conversation?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Since Commander Obrenovic had already spoken to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, he wanted to inform me as to what they were after, what their questions were like, and precisely for that reason, I asked him whether I should tell them what I knew, what I did, and then I mentioned specifically the cleansing operation at the school. However, he told me not to mention that. And that's more or less what was said in that conversation. He asked me where I'd been, where I was, what my obligations had been, what I'd done, and my impression was that I was actually being investigated by him in order for him to learn what was going on in Petkovci, whether I'd seen this person or the other, whether I'd gone to the school at all. And I told him everything that I stated in my statement. I don't know what his objective was. It's hard for me to assume what it might have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, Madam Nikolic seems to have something.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we have a mistake in the interpretation, page 27, line 21 in B/C/S, I heard it clearly that the witness said, "cleansing of the school" and in the transcript we had, "the cleansing operation at the school".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said, "cleanup of the school".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that resolves the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, as you sit here, why did Obrenovic tell you not to mention the bodies and the cleaning of the school?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Why he asked me not to mention this is very difficult for me to say. It's very difficult for me to put myself in his shoes and speculate what he meant by that. However, he insisted on me not mentioning it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you remember during your interview with the office of the Prosecution when that exact question was asked of you on page 50, your answer was as follows, and it's in the middle of the page on page 50. I'll read the question from Dean Manning: "Why did Obrenovic tell you not to mention the bodies and the cleaning of the school?" Answer by yourself, Mr. Ostoja Stanisic: "He just said that this should not be mentioned because this would maybe compromise the brigade and the command but this came spontaneously." Do you remember, sir, that you actually told the office of the Prosecution approximately five years ago that you remembered why Mr. Obrenovic told you not to mention, and that the answer you gave was the answer that I just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I remember that answer, but that was just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, who came up with this "spontaneously"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was just thinking aloud. Maybe that was what I was thinking, that the brigade should not be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Stanisic, before you testified or are testifying here today, it's my understanding from my learned friend that you had an opportunity to review your second statement as well as your other statements, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's my understanding from the office of the Prosecution that you had no changes and are going to stick to now this second version because it was different from the first interview, that you were going to stay with this second version, correct, and that you had no changes or corrections, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read your answer back again with respect to what Mr. Obrenovic may have said. Your answer sir and I'm quoting it here: "He just said that this should not be mentioned because this would maybe compromise the brigade and the command. But this came spontaneously." You're telling me and us today that that was your spontaneous thought and five years ago you didn't share with the Prosecution that in fact that is what you recalled Mr. Obrenovic said and that Mr. Obrenovic said it spontaneously, is that what you want to us believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It's a convoluted question, multi-part question and it's getting towards engaging in an argument. And if counsel could also lower his voice, he's awful close to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's check with Mr. Stanisic, did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was just going to ask for the question to be rephrased. Because I really cannot grasp the meaning of your question. What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I will and I'll keep my voice down but if I have the earphones on I can't hear it so that's the complexity of it. Mr. Stanisic I'm confused by your answer that you gave in 2002 and the answer that you're trying to give us today. And all I want is some simple clarification on that. Are you telling us under oath today that Mr. Obrenovic did not say that you must not mention the bodies and the prisoners because it would compromise the brigade and the command, or did he say that to you, as you testified and informed the office of the Prosecution both yesterday and five years ago?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Could you please take that slowly? It's just too fast. I can't follow you. You lost me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was speaking fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make questions simpler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I also -- excuse me just one second, the interviews at Banja Luka are not testimony. I know that's not -- but that may become relevant about testimony or statement later on. So if we could not refer that as testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How would I -- With the Court's permission, if the Court can ask the Prosecution how would he like me to refer to the interviews? Or statements or -- statements? Whatever his pleasure is, I just want to keep it consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Interview statements would be fine. We don't have a grand jury. There was no court there, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you gave your interview to the office of the Prosecution in 2002, were you telling them the truth?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you met with the Prosecutor a couple days ago, or yesterday, and you read your testimony from -- your statement from 2002, and you told them that you had no changes or corrections to it, was that also the truth?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, knowing from your testimony -- from your testimony here today and the statement that you gave in 2002, did Mr. Obrenovic tell you that you should not mention the bodies and the cleaning of the school because this would compromise the brigade and the command?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you mentioned in your interview statement of 2002 that from time to time you heard rumours and other sources, and that's on page 61 of his interview of 2002, that you heard rumours and stories and that you were actively following the newspaper and media in connection with the development of the Srebrenica trial. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: You'll have to repeat this again. Were you asking me whether I was actively following something?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll restate the question with the Court's permission. Sir, on page 61 of your 2002 interview, you informed the office of the Prosecution that you learned many things afterwards, and that you had heard rumours, stories, you read from various newspapers, and listened to various media outlets in connection with the Srebrenica issues that had developed since 1995. Did you in fact listen and hear about these stories and did you read from the newspaper and watch TV regarding the developments at issue after Srebrenica July 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, a lot of the information I learned from the newspapers, from General Krstic's trial. How shall I put it? When there are celebrations and festivities, people talk about these things. But those are all stories. This is all hearsay, something that is circulated on the grapevine. By the time it reaches me, God knows what the original story might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you remember reading any books on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. A book was published in which two people had escaped from the Brana and Crveni Mulj. This is their story.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember whether or not you followed or heard any of the developments from the Blagojevic trial? You mentioned Krstic but you didn't mention Blagojevic. Did you follow that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any -- do you know if your former deputy, Marko Milosevic, testified in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, during the second interview process with the office of the Prosecution, did you feel at all threatened or intimidated?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't feel threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember during the second interview with the office of the Prosecution, that Mr. Dean Manning, among others, insisted and instructed you on numerous occasions to tell the truth and actually doubted that you were telling them the truth? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you remember ultimately, or at one point, that Dean Manning or the Prosecutor who was there at the time said, on page 29, Your Honour, and counsel, on page 29 of said interview, "I don't think anyone would be able to believe your version." Do you remember being told that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the Prosecutor even prior to that instructing you to be frank, and that's on page 19, I'm sorry, to be frank and then also that they didn't believe what you said to them was true?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you also know -- recall that on page 28, the Prosecutor or the investigator at the time, and I believe it was Mr. Manning, on page 28, said, "You expect us to believe that there were only ten people in your command after you had that discussion?" And you responded by saying you expect us to believe that? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to that last comment, just so that we are clear, the headquarters of the 6th Battalion was located at what is commonly referred to as the old school in Petkovci, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it was your -- and it's your statement today, is it not, that on July 14th, 1995, purportedly there were only ten people at this old school at the 6th Battalion headquarters, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think if I recall your testimony -- or your statement properly, there were some elderly people there, a cook or two, and some wounded people as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I did not mention the wounded. What I meant were these people, my deputy, myself, three or four men who were elderly, who stood guard, and brought food, cooks and the signalsman, and that amounts to some ten people or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the name of the signalsman, if you will?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who the signalsman was. I had six of them, and I can't remember their names. I might be able to recall some of their nicknames, though. It was a long time ago. I never see them. And it's only natural that I've forgotten their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you remember the names of any of those ten people who were purportedly at the 6th Battalion headquarters known as old school, other than your deputy? Such as the elderly people who were standing guard, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't know their names. The cook was there. He resides in Trsic, I believe. What his name was, we used to call him Miki. I really can't remember. Really, I can't. I can't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one question that I failed to ask you about your meeting with Mr. Obrenovic. Did he -- actually two questions. Did he have -- was he taking notes during your meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: He did have a pen, and a notebook in front of him. He did make some notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he at that time also had with him the Zvornik Brigade duty officer logbook, notebook, I think is we are trying to call it consistently because we have used inconsistent words, which I think is P0377, for the record, of course. Do you know if he had the notebook, the duty officer's notebook from the Zvornik Brigade at the time that you had this meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple questions before the break. Sir, do you remember if Dean Manning ever told you -- and this is on page 4 -- whether he had intercepts of your radio communications?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That my conversation was recorded? No. But he did mention that there were a lot of intercepts that were recorded, but he never mentioned me as having been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: On any of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could just clarify that. On page 4, Dean Manning, among other things, states, "Intercepts of your radio conversations." And it goes on of course but just for purposes of this limited question, do you remember that he said he had intercepts of your radio conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. I think in order for the whole context to be understood, you should read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you suggested that you would be able to produce his statement or interview statement in B/C/S during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes. We have it, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's better for the witness to have his statement in front of him to answer those questions. If you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course I agree with you, Mr. President. I just was testing his recollection on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about taking a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has the witness been provided with his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We -- or at least I didn't understand to give him the statement. We found the statement. It is in e-court but he can be given the statement. We have it here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I would like to ask you, were you ever shown by Dean Manning or the Office of the Prosecution any intercepts of radio communications that you may have been mentioned in or were involved in?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, as I said earlier, and I think it's on 7D266, on the English version, page 4, and on the B/C/S version, it's page 5, but I think what's in the e-court is a mixed version of both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how that happens from time to time but it was produced by another team, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have a hard copy it would be easier for the witness to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do. Fair enough. With the Court's permission, if the usher can hand this to the witness? Please show it to my learned friend first. Page 5, if I may direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the parties and the Bench can follow from what you're saying but just give it to the witness so that he can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe what we've given you is a translated version of your interview of 2002, and before the break I was asking you, and it's just a quick question, Dean Manning, according to at least the English transcript that I have, page 4, states as follows: "What I want to know from you now and bearing in mind that we have not -- that we have not only those vehicle records but records from the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade, aerial images of the execution as it happened, intercepts of your radio conversations, radio conversations with the Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade and the Drina Corps, we have survivors from the dom itself, people who weren't executed, who managed to escape." He goes on and I'll read it just for completion of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could correct. That's a -- it's meant to be "dam", not "dom".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he continues to state, "So what I'm saying to you is that we have a large amount of information that points us in this direction and I want you to appreciate that before you answer." Did you find that section, sir, in your interview?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Did Dean Manning or anyone from the Office of the Prosecution ever share with you this "aerial images of the execution as it happened"?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. Never. It was never shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to clarify a couple other points, aside from your statement, so I don't think we need it at this point any more but it can remain with you, Mr. Witness, if the president and the Chamber so agrees. I want to ask you, in your 6th Battalion, were there any individuals with the first name Ljubo, as either a nickname or a full name? In July of 1995, obviously, sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, there probably were people by the name of Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ljubo Stojanovic. Stojanovic, I think. I'm going to go first and then I'll go to Bojanovic next, if I may. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Not by the name. I may know this person by sight but --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Ljubo Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him. He died.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a person named Ljubo Beatovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The last name Beatovic sounds familiar but Ljubo Beatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a name Ljubo Sobot?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a Ljubo Sobot who may have been a colonel in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can have for the witness P0377 which is the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook shown to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The notebook or logbook?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I was informed last night by my learned friend Mr. Thayer that we should try to call it a little consistently and he recommended that we call it by notebook as did Mr. McCloskey this morning so I'll call it whatever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just trying to accommodate them. If we can turn specifically to page -- which is on the entry of the 13th of July and it's page 2 of the English translation, and on the B/C/S it's the last ERN numbers 5739. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On that page, sir, do you see it in front of you, it's the third paragraph, if you will, of that page, which has ERN number 5739 do you see that entry where it starts with "Stojanovic, Ljubomir"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it states in English, at the very least, that this individual Ljubomir Stojanovic was to provide food. Does it say that or can you read it to us, for us?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: "Stojanovic, Ljubomir, provides food for SR." Now, I don't know if this is the first or the second PB, for the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I just wanted to confirm that this Ljubomir Stojanovic was providing food for the SR, as you say, that it states, and do you know if this conversation on the 13th of July, 1995, was purportedly captured by various Muslim intercept operators?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will address that later. Thank you for that. Sir, let me direct your attention to a map or a picture that you drew for the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of March 2001. It has ERN number 02171667, and with the Court's permission the usher can place it on the ELMO. Thank you. Now, just quickly if we may with this exhibit, sir, can you identify first of all what this is?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Here, we can see a sketch of the new school building, the battalion command. It's part of Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And this is something, sir, that you drew, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in fact your signature appears on the left-hand side of this drawing, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As well as the date. And underneath I'm not sure if it matters but Dean Manning's signature as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when you testified -- when you were interviewed and gave evidence to the Office of the Prosecution in 2002, this is -- it says 2001. This was a sketch that you were showing them where the command was, and you've identified it as such, I think in B/C/S, you write, "komanda", which is command. Underneath you put that it's the old school, "stara skola", do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side you have an arrow pointing to what seems to be a vacant area as the "igraliste", correct, the playground or --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you also identify the "nova skola", which is the new school, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you identify the two crossroads, do you not?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, you made a circle by this crossroad five or so years ago, maybe six now, and the circle indicated where you and Mr. -- where you claimed that Mr. Milosevic purportedly told you he encountered Mr. Beara on the 14th of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to compare that to what the Prosecution had you draw today in their picture. Now, do you agree with me that this picture that you drew more accurately identifies where you recall and where you recalled at that time that which Mr. Milosevic told you where he supposedly met Mr. Beara, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Here we see the same intersection as on the picture where I marked it. You have the same intersection. It's the same thing, the same intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll examine that. Thank you. Sir, what I wanted to ask you also was, and I don't believe my learned friend asked you this question, when Mr. Milosevic went towards the meadow to purportedly convey a message to Mr. Beara, did he drive?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: He went there on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he returned within a half hour, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I don't believe this was asked on direct but isn't it true that at one time or another, you claimed that you then called the brigade to inform him that the message to Mr. Beara was conveyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I notified the duty operations officer in the brigade that the message had been relayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, sir, that the custom and practice -- thank you, Madam Usher. That the custom and practice of the duty officer at the brigade was to record such purported conversations that you may have had with them, informing them that you have conveyed a certain message to an individual?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, he should have written that down, but much would depend on the duty officer in question. It would also depend on whether he was supposed to forward this information to anyone or was it just for his information. He perhaps should have noted this down, this message.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look at the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook on the 12th, for example, on page 7 in the English version, it clearly says that if there was any information to be conveyed, the duty officer on the 12th of July, for example, to the 4th and 7th Battalion, he identifies and says, "The 4th and 7th Battalion were informed." And it's my suggestion to you, sir, that at all times, as reflected in the duty officer notebook, such as July 12th, 15th, 16th, 17th and so on, that each time any request for things even such as mortar support, messages to be conveyed, looking for specific individuals, if someone calls back, they specifically identify and say, "Message conveyed." Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to intervene. I'm not sure whether the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll break it down. I was trying to simplify it in the interests of time, Your Honour. If we could have the logbook, please, brought up? If we could look to July 12th, for the Court and my learned friend, we are looking at page 7 of July 12th, of the translated version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it states, sir, on page 7 and I'll just read it to you and by the time we get it up in the transcript he's looking for it now, the exact page number, it says, if I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It says, "At 4.42, Lovac 1 reported, informed the 4th and 7th to pay special attention to their back." Immediately underneath that or after it, it says, "The 4th and 7th PB were informed immediately." I'm just highlighting for you, sir, that if they informed someone of something they would record whether or not that person was actually informed or advised. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you're driving at. Whether the duty operations officer noted down what I told him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I think the witness has answered in a general manner. Could we -- the logbook, the notebook is there. Can we not proceed and move on to another subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I can just ask one other question and I am proceeding on this, if we could look at ERN number of the notebook 5764, which is in English the last four numbers, 9359.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And towards the bottom of that page, 5764, if we may scroll down, on the bottom of that page, do you see, sir, where at 1120 hours, it says "Badem, Colonel Jankovic was looking for Major Malinic". Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does it say after that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: "To call him." I can't decipher this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the English version it says, "Message conveyed."

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: "Conveyed".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, that nowhere in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook is there any indication that you called purportedly the duty officer to inform him that you had conveyed a message to Mr. Beara on the 14th of July 1995. And the reason for that, sir, is because you're simply not telling us the truth and you did not convey a message to Mr. Beara through your deputy.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, that, I think, is your opinion. I cannot agree with it. Now, whether the duty officer noted that down or not, I can't bring him here, I cannot confront him here and ask him why you didn't sign -- why didn't you note this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And, sir, you never saw Mr. Beara himself either at the Zvornik command, at the Petkovci old school or at the new school personally, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear because it's a double negative sometimes this happens, I'm correct you did not, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple questions about your first name, Ostoja. Was there another Ostoja in the battalion in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission I've been notified that the full question wasn't recorded. I'm sure it's my fault so if I can restate it or should we just allow for the transcript to be corrected as they do it from time to time in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was because you overlapped with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Clearly it was my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just in case, why don't you repeat your question for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, or Mr. Stanisic, I'm sorry, I asked you a question and you answered it. It was not captured on the transcript. I apologise for having to ask the question again. But I'll ask it: Sir, am I correct that in July of 1995, you never saw Mr. Ljubisa Beara himself anywhere near or around the Zvornik command, the Petkovci old school or the Petkovci new school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look with you this one intercept that we've been having some trouble with and I think you might be able to help me. Do you remember what the code-name was for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the code-name was for Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. Because as a battalion commander, I did not communicate directly with the brigades, with the exception of my brigade, and usually it would be encrypted for the purpose of radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Vojanovic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Vojanovic? I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where or what -- where in relation to Snagovo is Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It is west of Snagovo, more to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Snagovo earlier in your testimony today. Am I correct that you were asked to bring men and you sent them to the Standard so that they could go to Snagovo and the reason for that is because the Bosnian Muslims were pushing your guys back towards Crni Vrh? Is that accurate? And that's why they needed reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I stated in my previous statement that reinforcements had been sought in order to set up a unit to defend the town of Zvornik, and the Serb villages at Snagovo, simply to oppose the enemy, to prevent the enemy from attacking the town or the Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can have the intercept which we don't have in e-court, Your Honour, and I think it might take a second but we can probably give him a clean copy that's already been tendered by the Prosecution of the 14th of July 1995, which bears ERN number 01043214, and this quite candidly came up because the witness testified for the first time, at least based on my recollection, that he understood RUP as the evidence was led by my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecution. And this is an intercept with the time 2102 hours. Even though I have some markings on it, unless -- may I show him that? Maybe I could show it to my learned friend and he can see if he has an objection to the markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just got the number on e-court, 1164. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Small a, b, c?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We can have both the English and the B/C/S version so I think it would be a and b, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A is English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 1164D, D as in dog.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before putting this to the witness, can I ask Mr. McCloskey whether it would be okay to put this document, which is confidential, to the witness, in particular the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could see what we are talking about, I don't think it's a particular problem. I mean if it's initials it's not a problem. I don't know what else it might be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Name of the place or -- I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, the reason I think the first name that appears on this intercept is identical to this gentleman's first name and I wanted to clarify because we did have some issues, with all due respect, with this intercept, the operator himself at the end of the intercept identifies that it may or may not have been intercepted or interrupted and I wanted to clarify if he recalls --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Could we not have these discussions in front of the witness? All I think we are worried about is identifying the intercept operator and if that is not a problem with the exhibit which I don't see, then I think we can show it to him with no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. If the Prosecution is in agreement, let's put it, proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did we -- were we able to put on the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not broadcast this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, in this document, it has -- do you see reference to the first name Ostoja? Do you see that? And this is the printed version, although I think from time to time we also used the written version of this document. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I can't see it. Where, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you look on the -- right on the 4th entry on the left which says, J, and then four lines below that it has the name --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And above that --

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And above that, two lines to the right, it has the name Ostoja again, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It says, "Is there Ostoja, who is Ostoja? Is Ostoja there? Can you pass him on to me?"

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall a conversation with Major Jokic on or about the 14th of July 1994, at 210 -- 1995, at 2102 hours where you discuss with him Snagovo and the reason why he needed men in Snagovo was because the Muslims have pushed your guys back toward Crni Vrh? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: This is not clear. The name Ostoja is mentioned but I don't remember this conversation at all. Is there Ostoja? Is there Brko? In my battalion, I did not have a Brko.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, what extension 155 is?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know to whom extension 155 belongs to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know where extension 155 is located at?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We don't need that document any longer. Sir, quite candidly, I would like to suggest to you in the few moments that we have that during your two and a half hour ride with Mr. Milosevic, for your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002, you and he both concocted this story to say that Mr. Beara was near or around a meadow towards the new school on July 14th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with what you're saying. What I've stated is the truth. I got a call from the brigade that Colonel Beara should report to a command, Milosevic conveyed that message, there was no previous agreement on that on our part. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, when you met with Mr. Josic, I suggest to you that you also concocted and created the story with Mr. Josic with respect to the lorries and the trucks that were being used to transport some of the dead bodies that were located at the school. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. Again, I don't agree with you. I stand by what I've stated, which is the following: The lorry that was driven by Josic went to Srebrenica and returned on the 16th. Many can confirm that fact, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And give me the names of some of those many, sir.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Acimovic can confirm it. His name is Mladen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Mladen Acimovic prior to giving an interview or testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Privately, we did meet on several occasions but we never discussed this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to accept this as a proposition for my follow-up question, that in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook, on numerous occasions, when someone requests that a message be conveyed, and if that message is indeed conveyed, the duty officer would record that in his notebook. Can you tell me why, for the period of July 14th, 1995, there is no such record whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. That's been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like for him to reconcile it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. He answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me why it is that only you and Mr. Milosevic purport to be the only individuals from all those in your battalion that claim to know that there was this purported request for Mr. Beara and that that request was purportedly conveyed to him to report to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Assumes facts not in evidence. I don't think there is any -- been established that they are the only one that know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could restate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe it's taken as his suggestion and whether -- the question can be taken whether he would agree with it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Why nobody from the 6th Battalion, from among the troops or anybody else, saw Colonel Beara? From my testimony, you could conclude where people were, who could have seen him, who was in the command and how far the school is from the command. Nobody was able to see him. Maybe many did see him. But maybe they didn't know him, they didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question maybe another way, if I may. Do you know of any individual other than yourself and Mr. Milosevic who claim that Mr. Beara was at or near the intersection by the new school?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you a question that was followed up by my learned friend towards the end of his direct examination. Is it your testimony that on the 15th of July 1995, some unknown person called you and they requested that additional prisoners be brought to the school and that you said no, and that ultimately those prisoners were not brought to the school; correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask you this while you're under oath. Why, if you knew that the prisoners were coming to the school on the 14th of July 1995, why didn't you say no at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, I didn't know that they were coming to the school. When I returned from the forward command post, i.e. from the defence sector, they were already in the school. My deputy had received information that soldiers were supposed to arrive at the school. How should I have refused that given the fact that they had already been there in the school, even before I returned from my defence position?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple more questions with respect to Mr. Obrenovic. Do you have any information, sir, about the fact that Mr. Obrenovic may have entered certain dates in the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook with pencil? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear that from anyone, a rumour or a story?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that when SFOR went to obtain the Zvornik Brigade documents in 1998, correct, you knew that they did that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook was not among those documents but that that specific notebook was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor a couple, if not several or a few years after the attempt and seizure by SFOR in 1998 of the Zvornik Brigade? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who had possession of the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook for those two to four years prior to the time that the Prosecution received it, but after the seizure by SFOR?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, SFOR didn't seize it, if we could just get the OTP --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. In his statement he actually I think in the 2001 statement referred to it as being SFOR so I didn't want to complicate it by showing him his statement but the OTP seizure is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness can be asked who had possession of the duty officer's notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. May I restate the question, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what was taken from the brigade. I only know that those who had collected the documents said that everything was taken away. Whatever remained was out of my reach because I was in another barracks as a battalion commander. I was not in the brigade command. So I'm not in a position to tell you what remained behind and where the documents that might have remained behind were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, just so I'm clear because I asked you about this intercept, on 14th July 1995 at 2100 hours, you were never in Bratunac, correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I suggest to you, sir, that having watched the Krstic trial and having these meetings with Obrenovic and Josic and Milosevic, that in fact, sir, as early as 2000 and specifically in 2002, you and these other individuals, including Obrenovic, decided to come up and create a story which would purportedly absolve you of any culpability or responsibility and you sought to shift that blame on others, specifically the security staff. Am I correct on that, aren't I?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Again, that is your personal view. I don't agree with that. I, as a member of the army, when I was an active officer and especially now, when I'm a mere civilian, I have never conspired with anybody against anybody, and particularly in those things that you claim that I continuously followed the trial. You are mistaken there as well. Only in one of my statements did I say that the first person who was ever found responsible or punished was Krstic. I never said that I followed the entire trial and everything. I believe that your opinion of me is completely wrong and for that reason, I can't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, my opinion of you is that which the Prosecutor had in 2002 on page 29, when they say they don't think anyone would be able to believe your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. That was not a question. It's just a little crack, as he's leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reserve your opinion to a later stage. So you're done with your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have more but given the hour I think it might be a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're done for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll continue tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may. I'll look over everything and consult and we'll let the Court know tomorrow. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may have noticed, Your Honour, when I was getting out the second vehicle log there was a foul-up and we didn't have what I needed on the computer. We've fixed it and it's now there. I just wanted to make sure counsel had the correct vehicle log, and if I could have one question to reopen my examination, perhaps tomorrow, or I can come in after everybody, just to ask about that second vehicle log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would there be any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no objection, we saw he was looking for the document and it would be fair, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So for the first thing tomorrow you ask that question to be followed by the Defence. Very well, we will adjourn. We will sit tomorrow at 9.00, but Mr. Stanisic, probably you may have been informed but you are not to discuss your evidence with other people during the break. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
